claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS (AWS-only) and is AWS-centric.
Multi-cloud is nearly impossible with AWS CDK; AWS CDK supports AWS only.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python (language support comparison table).
Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging whereas AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK due to direct execution, while CDK is slower due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility, whereas AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployment.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments supports more advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi has upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new SST deployment engine; its constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console; the Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST potentially has supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

SST's published platform/package.json depends on `@pulumi/pulumi` plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository (formerly `sst/sst`) lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside other tools, and the same provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer.

Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments", with official Nitric providers built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its pulumi-defang provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.

Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, users can define resources directly in Pulumi inside an SST app for anything lacking a dedicated SST construct and deploy them as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per the npm API).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub star following than SST itself.
The SST team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or the framework's dependency on the Pulumi engine.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally by a platform team, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be adopted by an SST user without leaving the Pulumi engine SST already uses.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST is a strong fit for teams wanting an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together.
SST's abstractions are enough for a lot of teams and applications.
Writing a correct provisioning engine is a bigger project than it looks from the outside and is expensive to get right.
The related post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
